text: Laura Phillips "Laurie" Anderson, born on June 5, 1947, in Chicago and raised in Glen Ellyn, Illinois, one of eight children of Mary Louise (née Rowland) and Arthur T. Anderson, is an American avant-garde artist, musician, and filmmaker whose work spans performance art, pop music, and multimedia projects. Initially trained in violin and sculpting, she pursued performance art in New York City during the 1970s, focusing on language, technology, and visual imagery. Her first performance-art piece, a symphony played on automobile horns, was performed in 1969. In 1970, she drew the underground comix Baloney Moccasins, published by George DiCaprio. She worked as an art instructor and art critic for Artforum and illustrated children's books, including The Package (1971), a picture-only mystery. In the early 1970s, she performed in New York, with one of her most-cited works, Duets on Ice, involving her playing the violin while wearing ice skates with blades frozen into ice, ending only when the ice melted. Two early pieces, "New York Social Life" and "Time to Go," were included in the 1977 compilation New Music for Electronic and Recorded Media, along with works by Pauline Oliveros, and two others appeared on Airwaves. She recorded a lecture for Vision, a set of artist's lectures released by Crown Point Press as six LPs. Many of her earliest recordings remain unreleased or were issued in limited quantities, such as "It's Not the Bullet that Kills You (It's the Hole)," originally recorded for a jukebox art installation at the Holly Solomon Gallery in New York City, featuring musicians Peter Gordon, Scott Johnson, Ken Deifik, and Joe Kos. In the late 1970s, she released recordings through the Giorno Poetry Systems label, and in 1977, she was granted an artist-in-residence stay at the Cité internationale des Arts in Paris. In 1978, she performed at the Nova Convention, which included notable figures like William S. Burroughs, Philip Glass, Frank Zappa, Timothy Leary, Malcolm Goldstein, John Cage, and Allen Ginsberg. She also worked with comedian Andy Kaufman in the late 1970s. In 1980, she received an honorary doctorate from the San Francisco Art Institute; in 1982, she was awarded a Guggenheim Fellowship for Creative Arts—Film; and in 1987, she received an honorary doctorate in the fine arts from the University of the Arts in Philadelphia. She gained widespread recognition in 1981 with the single "O Superman," originally released by B. George's One Ten Records in limited quantity, which reached number two on the UK singles chart, prompting a surge in orders that led to a seven-album contract with Warner Bros. Records, which re-released the single. "O Superman" was part of the stage work United States Live (1984) and appeared on her debut studio album Big Science (1982). Prior to Big Science, she recorded the collaboration album You're the Guy I Want to Share My Money With (1981) with William S. Burroughs and John Giorno, with each artist recording one side of a double-LP and a separate groove on the fourth side. This was followed by the back-to-back releases of Mister Heartbreak and United States Live (both 1984), the latter a five-LP (and later four-CD) recording of her two-evening stage show at the Brooklyn Academy of Music. She also appeared in a television special produced by Nam June Paik, "Good Morning, Mr. Orwell," broadcast on New Year's Day 1984. She starred in and directed the 1986 concert film Home of the Brave and composed soundtracks for the Spalding Gray films Swimming to Cambodia (1987) and Monster in a Box (1992). She contributed music to Robert Wilson's Alcestis at the American Repertory Theater in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and hosted the PBS series Alive from Off Center in 1987 after producing the short film What You Mean We? the year before. In that film, she introduced "The Clone," a digitally altered masculine counterpart to her, who later co-hosted with her on Alive from Off Center. Elements of the Clone were later used in the puppet of her later work, Puppet Motel. In 1991, she was a member of the jury at the 41st Berlin International Film Festival. That year, she appeared in The Human Face, a BBC documentary on the history of the face in art and science, where her face was transformed using latex masks and digital effects. In 1994, she created a CD-ROM titled Puppet Motel, followed by Bright Red, co-produced by Brian Eno, and a spoken-word album, The Ugly One with the Jewels (1995). In 1997, she appeared on the charity single "Perfect Day." In 1996, she performed with Diego Frenkel (La Portuária) and Aterciopelados for the AIDS benefit album Silencio=Muerte: Red Hot + Latin produced by the Red Hot Organization. After a more than half-decade gap, she released her next album in 1999 with Songs and Stories from Moby Dick. During this time, she wrote a supplemental article on the cultural character of New York City for the Encyclopædia Britannica and created multimedia presentations, including one inspired by Moby-Dick. A central theme in her work is the exploration of technology's effects on human relationships and communication. Starting in the 1990s, she collaborated with Lou Reed, whom she met in 1992, on recordings: Reed contributed to "In Our Sleep" (Bright Red, 1994), "One Beautiful Evening" (Life on a String, 2001), "My Right Eye" and "Only an Expert" (Homeland, 2010), which he also co-produced; Anderson contributed to "Call on Me" (The Raven, 2003), "Rouge" and "Rock Minuet" (Ecstasy, 2000), and "Hang On to Your Emotions" (Set the Twilight Reeling, 1996). In late 1998, Artist Space in New York presented an exhibit of her work from the 1970s to 1980s, including her 1990s work Whirlwind. Life on a String was released in 2001, after she signed a new recording contract with Nonesuch Records, a Warner Music Group label. The album combined new works, including one recalling the death of her father, with material from the Moby-Dick presentation. In 2001, she recorded the audiobook version of Don DeLillo's novella The Body Artist and toured performing her best-known musical pieces, including a performance of "O Superman" in New York City a week after the September 11 attacks, released in early 2002 as the double CD Live in New York. In 2003, she produced albums with French musicians La Jarry and Hector Zazou and performed with them; Zazou's album Strong Currents (2003) featured her alongside Jane Birkin, Lori Carson, and Irene Grandi. In 2003, she became NASA's first artist-in-residence, which inspired her performance piece The End of the Moon. In May 2004, she received an honorary doctorate from Columbia University. She was part of the team that created the opening ceremony for the 2004 Summer Olympics in Athens and collaborated with choreographer Trisha Brown and filmmaker Agnieszka Wojtowicz-Vosloo on the multimedia project O Zlozony/O Composite, which premiered at the Palais Garnier in Paris in December 2004. She mounted themed shows and composed a piece for Expo 2005 in Japan. In 2005, she visited Russia's space program, including the Gagarin Cosmonaut Training Centre and mission control, with Arts Catalyst and participated in the Arts Catalyst's Space Soon event at the Roundhouse. Her exhibition The Waters Reglitterized opened at the Sean Kelly Gallery in New York City in 2005, described as a diary of dreams and their literal recreation as art, including drawings, prints, and high-definition video, running until October 22, 2005. In 2006, she was awarded a residency at the American Academy in Rome and narrated Ric Burns' Andy Warhol: A Documentary Film, first televised in September 2006 as part of the PBS American Masters series. She contributed a song to Plague Songs, a collection of songs related to the 10 Biblical plagues, and performed at Came So Far for Beauty, a Leonard Cohen tribute event in Dublin, Ireland, on October 4–5, 2006. In November 2006, she published a book of drawings based on her dreams, titled Night Life. Material from Homeland was performed in small work-in-progress shows in New York throughout May 2007, supported by a four-piece band with live lighting and video by Willie Williams and Mark Coniglio. A European tour included performances in Dublin (September 28–29, 2007), Melbourne (October 17–19, 2007), and Russia (April 26, 2008) at the Moscow Dom Muzyky. The work was performed in Toronto, Canada, on June 14, 2008, with her husband Lou Reed, making "The Lost Art of Conversation" a duet. The Homeland Tour included performances at the Ferst Center for the Arts in Atlanta, Georgia; The Lincoln Center for the Performing Arts in New York City; and the Harris Theater for Music and Dance in Chicago, Illinois, co-presented by the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago. In February 2010, she premiered a new theatrical work, Delusion, at the 2010 Winter Olympics in Vancouver, Canada, commissioned by the Vancouver 2010 Cultural Olympiad and the Barbican Centre, London. She received the Women's Project Theater Woman of Achievement Award in March 2010. In May–June 2010, she curated the Vivid Live festival in Sydney with Lou Reed. Her new studio album Homeland was released on June 22. She performed "Only an Expert" on July 15, 2010, on the Late Show with David Letterman, and her song "Gravity's Angel" was featured on the Fox reality television dance competition show So You Think You Can Dance the same day. She appears as a guest musician on several tracks from experimental jazz musician Colin Stetson's studio album New History Warfare Vol. 2: Judges (2011). In 2012, she developed a theatrical work titled "Another Day in America," with first public showings in Calgary, Alberta, Canada, in January 2012 as part of Theatre Junction Grand's 2011–12 season and One Yellow Rabbit's annual arts festival, the High Performance Rodeo. In May 2012, she was named the Inaugural Distinguished Artist-In-Residence at the Experimental Media and Performing Arts Center (EMPAC) at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute in Troy, New York. In March 2013, an exhibition titled Laurie Anderson: Language of the Future, selected works 1971–2013, was held at the Samstag Museum as part of the Adelaide Festival of the Arts in Adelaide, South Australia, with a performance of Duets on Ice on opening night. In 2013, she received the Honorary Doctor of Arts from the Aalto University School of Arts, Design and Architecture. In June/July 2013, she performed "The Language of the Future" and guest curated at the River to River Festival in New York City. In November 2013, she was the featured Guest of Honor at the B3 Biennale of the Moving Image in Frankfurt, Germany. In 2018, she contributed vocals to a re-recording of David Bowie's "Shining Star (Makin' My Love)," originally from Bowie's 1987 album Never Let Me Down, produced by Mario J. McNulty, who knew Anderson and Bowie were friends. On February 10, 2019, at the 61st Annual Grammy Awards in Los Angeles, Anderson and the Kronos Quartet's Landfall won the Grammy Award for Best Chamber Music/Small Ensemble Performance, marking her first Grammy and her first collaboration with the Kronos Quartet; the award was inspired by her experience of Hurricane Sandy, with Nonesuch Records noting the work juxtaposed lush electronics and traditional strings with Anderson's powerful descriptions of loss, from water-logged pianos to disappearing animal species to Dutch karaoke bars. Chalkroom is a virtual reality work by Anderson and Taiwanese artist Hsin-Chien Huang in which the reader flies through a structure made of words, drawings, and stories. To the Moon, a collaboration with Hsin-Chien Huang, premiered at the Manchester International Festival on July 12, 2019, as a 15-minute virtual reality artwork allowing audience members to explore a moon with donkey rides and Earth's rubbish in a non-narrative structure, accompanied by a film showing the development of the work. Laurie Anderson received her first Grammy Award in 2019 for her album *Landfall*, which was the second Grammy for Kronos and was inspired by her experience of Hurricane Sandy. The album, described by Nonesuch Records as juxtaposing lush electronics and traditional strings by Kronos with Anderson's powerful descriptions of loss—such as water-logged pianos, disappearing animal species, and Dutch karaoke bars—won the Grammy for Best Chamber Music/Small Ensemble Performance. In October 2012, Hurricane Sandy destroyed archives of her creative work, including photographs, performance props, audiovisual equipment, musical instruments, and other materials, which led to her writing the book *All the Things I Lost in the Flood* (2018) reflecting on her career and the ephemeral nature of art. Anderson moved to New York in 1966 and now lives in Tribeca; she met musician Lou Reed in 1992 and was married to him from April 2008 until his death in 2013. She is a foreign member of the Royal Swedish Academy of Music and a long-time student of Buddhism and meditation, having first learned meditation in 1977 with the Insight Meditation Society and later studying with Tibetan Nepali teacher Yongey Mingyur Rinpoche. Anderson invented several experimental instruments, including a tape-bow violin created in 1977 that uses recorded magnetic tape in the bow and a magnetic tape head in the bridge, which she has updated over the years and used in her film *Home of the Brave* with MIDI-based audio samples; and a six-foot-long baton-like MIDI controller called the "talking stick," developed in the late 1990s with Interval Research and Bob Bielecki, which uses granular synthesis to break sound into tiny segments called grains and reassemble them into new textures. A recurring motif in her work is the use of an electric pitch-shifting voice filter that deepens her voice into a masculine register, which she calls "audio drag." This voice, initially known as the "Voice of Authority" and later dubbed Fenway Bergamot at Lou Reed's suggestion, has been used as a "voice of authority" or conscience, and later as a tool for historical or sociopolitical commentary, as seen in "Another Day in America" from her 2010 album *Homeland*. In 2021, she was appointed the Charles Eliot Norton Professor of Poetry at Harvard University and delivered a series of six lectures titled *Spending the War Without You: Virtual Backgrounds* over two semesters. In 2021, she created a show titled *The Weather* at the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden in Washington, D.C., described by *The New York Times* as "a sort of nonretrospective retrospective of one of America's major, and majorly confounding, modern artists." In mid-2023, her exhibit *Looking into a Mirror Sideways*, highlighting various styles of her art techniques, opened at the Moderna Museet in Stockholm, Sweden, and became her biggest solo show in Europe. In 2024, she withdrew from a guest professorship at the Folkwang University of the Arts in Essen, Germany, after university officials objected to her support of a "Letter Against Apartheid" organized by Palestinian artists, calling for "an immediate and unconditional cessation of Israeli violence against Palestinians." In November 2024, she staged *United States V*, a multimedia performance envisioned as a sequel to *United States*, commissioned by Factory International and staged at Aviva Studios in Manchester, England, featuring video appearances from Ai Weiwei as God and Anohni as an angel. She also collaborated with Taiwanese artist Hsin-Chien Huang on *Chalkroom*, a virtual reality work where the reader flies through a structure made of words, drawings, and stories, and *To the Moon*, a 15-minute virtual reality artwork that premiered at the Manchester International Festival on July 12, 2019, allowing audience members to explore a moon with donkey rides and Earth's rubbish in a non-narrative structure, accompanied by a film showing its development. The single "Sharkey's Day" was for many years the theme song of the cable channel Lifetime, and she has contributed to recordings by Peter Gabriel, Lou Reed, Jean-Michel Jarre, Philip Glass, and a tribute album for John Cage. Formal music videos have been produced for her work, and in lieu of a music video for her *Strange Angels* album, she created a series of one- to two-minute "Personal Service Announcements" in the early 1990s, which were frequently shown between music videos on VH1 and used music from her *Swimming to Cambodia* soundtrack. In 2013, Dale Eisinger of Complex ranked *United States* as the third greatest work of performance art ever, noting Anderson's ability to capture the climate of life in the United States without causing a standoff, with her *United States I – IV* performances being highlighted as a peak of her range.
